finding.description: Describes a defect in the same-role review, not a candidate defect already captured by a supported review finding.

reviewFindingAdjudication.description: Judges one finding made by the same-role review rather than judging the candidate defect again.

findingIds.description: Links only adjudicator findings that explain why this review finding is rejected; this array is empty when judgment is supported.

surfaceAdjudication.description: Echoes the bound same-role review assessment in reviewAssessmentJudgment and judges the soundness of that assessment in judgment. A sound blocking review assessment is blocking plus supported, not an adjudication failure.

findingIds.description: Links only adjudicator findings that explain a rejected same-role review assessment. It is empty for supported; rejected requires a linked blocking finding on this surface.

judgment.description: supported approves the same-role review assessment even when reviewAssessmentJudgment is blocking; rejected means the assessment is unsound or incomplete.

reviewAssessmentJudgment.description: Exact echo of the bound same-role review assessment's judgment; the deterministic verifier rejects any mismatch.

adjudicationSchema.description: This record judges the soundness and completeness of the same-role review, not the candidate.

findings.description: Adjudicator findings describe defects in the same-role review's requirement, assessment, reasoning, finding, coverage, or severity; they do not repeat candidate defects already captured by supported review findings.

reviewFindingAdjudications.description: Each entry judges one same-role review finding. A supported review finding has no adjudicator-finding links; a rejected review finding requires a linked blocking adjudicator finding that explains the review defect.

surfaceAdjudications.description: Each entry exactly echoes the same-role review assessment's pass, advisory, or blocking judgment, then separately judges that assessment as supported or rejected; it does not judge the candidate surface directly.

verdict.description: pass means the same-role review is sound and complete, even when that review correctly fails the candidate; fail means the same-role review is unsound or incomplete. This verdict never judges the candidate directly.

adjudicationSchema.title: Independent canonical-English semantic adjudication record

adjudicationSemantics.failMeaning: The same-role review is unsound or incomplete.
adjudicationSemantics.findingLinkMeaning: A supported surface assessment or review finding has no adjudicator-finding links; a rejected one links at least one blocking adjudicator finding on an overlapping surface that explains a defect in the review.
adjudicationSemantics.passMeaning: The same-role review is sound and complete, even when that review correctly fails the candidate.
adjudicationSemantics.subject: same-role-review
adjudicationSemantics.surfaceAdjudicationMeaning: Each surface adjudication exactly echoes the bound review assessment judgment in reviewAssessmentJudgment, then uses judgment supported or rejected to judge that assessment.

class="lesson-back" href="/en/course/"> ← All chapters </a> <p class="eyebrow"> 00 · Content revision 6 </p> <h1>A map of the scalar reference decoder</h1> <p class="lesson-description">In the tiny CPU reference, tokenization gives IDs, embeddings give features, and decoder blocks plus a vocabulary head produce logits. Sampling selects tokens, caching reuses attention state, and training updates the same weights. This architectural map does not establish measured laptop-scale capability.</p> <aside class="lesson-objective"> <strong>In this chapter</strong> <p>Identify the major parts of a decoder-only LLM, understand how they connect, and use the course links to find the chapter that builds each part.</p> </aside>  </header> <div class="lesson-body"> 
<h2 id="see-the-system-before-its-mechanisms">See the system before its mechanisms</h2>
<p>A decoder-only LLM is easier to approach as a connected system than as one opaque
box. Prompt text first becomes token IDs. Embedding lookup turns those IDs into
learned features. A stack of decoder blocks repeatedly mixes information from the
allowed prefix and transforms the features at each position. A vocabulary head
then produces one score for every possible next token.</p>
<p>From those scores, the system can do two different jobs. During generation, a
decoding policy chooses a token ID, appends it to the sequence, and runs the model
again using the existing attention cache. During learning, the observed next token
acts as a target: loss measures the prediction, gradients assign responsibility,
and an optimizer changes the weights used by embeddings, decoder blocks, and the
vocabulary head.</p>
<p>The course implements these connections as a scalar reference: explicit CPU
loops operate on <code>f64</code> values so the computation can be inspected. Chapter 39
joins the parts in a tiny deterministic example. That example demonstrates how
the parts work together, not useful language quality or measured laptop-scale
training and inference.</p>
<p>This overview deliberately stops at names, purposes, and connections. Later
chapters derive the mathematics and build each mechanism in Rust when that detail
has a clear place in the model.</p>

<h2 id="a-short-road-to-the-modern-block-diagram">A short road to the modern block diagram</h2>
<p>Count n-grams condition on a fixed short context and cannot learn reusable
distributed features or content-dependent access to a longer prefix. Neural
language models learned distributed token representations, the Transformer
supplied masked self-attention over the prefix, and later autoregressive
Transformer language models scaled next-token prediction. A modern decoder-only
LLM repeatedly transforms token features with normalized causal attention and
gated feed-forward branches, then projects the result to a next-token distribution
used by learning or generation.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf">A Neural Probabilistic Language Model</a>
supports the earlier boundary. Bengio and colleagues contrast n-gram generalization
with a neural probability function that learns distributed word representations;
their model predates the Transformer and this course’s decoder block.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762">Attention Is All You Need</a> supports the later
architecture boundary. Vaswani and colleagues define the Transformer and mask
decoder self-attention against later positions; their published system is an
encoder-decoder model, not this course’s decoder-only topology.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.14165">Language Models are Few-Shot Learners</a> supports
the scaling boundary. Brown and colleagues describe GPT-3 as a scaled
autoregressive language model; its scale and measured capabilities do not transfer
to the tiny reference model used here.</p>

<h2 id="follow-the-blocks-as-one-connected-system">Follow the blocks as one connected system</h2>
<p>The first figure is the whole-system schema: a shared forward path reaches logits,
then generation and learning branch in different directions. Feedback arrows show
where a chosen token re-enters the model and where updated weights affect the next
learning step. The cache and numeric foundation sit beside the path because they
support model computation rather than acting as extra tokens in the sequence.</p>
<p>The second figure keeps the useful detailed views. Its three panels list the ordinary
inference stages, open the repeated decoder block, and separate the post-logit
learning operations. Every named part links to the chapter that implements it.</p>

<h2 id="use-the-map-as-a-table-of-contents">Use the map as a table of contents</h2>
<p>You do not need to memorize this map. Return to it whenever a later mechanism
feels isolated and ask only where that mechanism sits: before the decoder, inside
each repeated block, after logits, or in the process that trains and preserves the
weights.</p>
<p>Chapters 1 through 7 establish text, tokenization, causal examples, a count
baseline, and language-model metrics. Chapters 8 through 23 build the numeric and
learning foundation. Chapters 24 through 32 assemble the decoder. Chapters 33
through 38 train, evaluate, persist, sample, and cache it. Chapter 39 runs the
scalar reference end to end. The separately planned extension begins with
Chapter 40’s explanation of what this reference establishes and what later
laptop work must still demonstrate.</p>
<p>The evaluation node names a post-selection role, not a promise that every
repository run sees newly unopened data. Inside one execution, the local
evaluator cannot affect the selected state; repository reruns retain the known
result only as fixed-fixture regression evidence.</p>

<p>Chapter 1 begins the implementation path with the distinction every later block
depends on: text is not yet a model input. It must first become stable token IDs.

<h2 id="start-with-two-three-letter-inputs">Start with two three-letter inputs</h2>
<p>Rust stores both <code>cat</code> and <code>кот</code> as UTF-8, but equal-looking lengths do not imply
equal byte lengths. Before reading the table, predict three counts for each input:
its bytes, its Unicode scalar values, and its vocabulary IDs.</p>






























<table><thead><tr><th style="text-align:left">Representation</th><th style="text-align:left"><code>cat</code></th><th style="text-align:left"><code>кот</code></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td style="text-align:left">UTF-8 bytes</td><td style="text-align:left"><code>[99, 97, 116]</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>[208, 186, 208, 190, 209, 130]</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">Unicode scalar values</td><td style="text-align:left"><code>[U+0063, U+0061, U+0074]</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>[U+043A, U+043E, U+0442]</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">Vocabulary IDs</td><td style="text-align:left"><code>[3, 2, 4]</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>[5, 6, 7]</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left">Decoded text</td><td style="text-align:left"><code>cat</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>кот</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>The result is <code>3 / 3 / 3</code> for <code>cat</code> and <code>6 / 3 / 3</code> for <code>кот</code>. Each Cyrillic
scalar occupies two UTF-8 bytes here, but both inputs still contain three scalar
positions and produce three IDs.</p>
<p>The IDs come from one fixed training string, <code>cat кот</code>. ID <code>0</code> is reserved for
<code><UNK></code>; known scalar values are sorted by numeric Unicode value and receive IDs
from <code>1</code>:</p>


















































<table><thead><tr><th style="text-align:right">ID</th><th style="text-align:center">Unit</th><th style="text-align:left">Unicode value</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td style="text-align:right">0</td><td style="text-align:center"><code><UNK></code></td><td style="text-align:left">unknown</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:right">1</td><td style="text-align:center">space</td><td style="text-align:left"><code>U+0020</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:right">2</td><td style="text-align:center"><code>a</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>U+0061</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:right">3</td><td style="text-align:center"><code>c</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>U+0063</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:right">4</td><td style="text-align:center"><code>t</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>U+0074</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:right">5</td><td style="text-align:center"><code>к</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>U+043A</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:right">6</td><td style="text-align:center"><code>о</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>U+043E</code></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:right">7</td><td style="text-align:center"><code>т</code></td><td style="text-align:left"><code>U+0442</code></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>This rule is deterministic: it does not depend on hash-map iteration order. The
round trip is reversible for known units. For the unseen input <code>?</code>, byte <code>63</code> and
scalar <code>U+003F</code> are observable before lookup, but encoding produces <code>[0]</code> and
decoding returns <code><UNK></code> rather than the original question mark.</p>
<p>The concrete <code>Vocabulary</code> type is a deliberately small Chapter 1 comparison, not
the tokenizer used by later chapters. It assigns a distinct ID to each known
Unicode scalar value. Its fixed table therefore makes the mapping easy to inspect,
while its single <code><UNK></code> ID also exposes the cost of incomplete coverage.</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>Key idea:</strong> UTF-8 byte count and token-sequence length measure different units. This demo emits one ID per Unicode scalar, so its token-sequence length equals its scalar count, while only scalars present in the fixed vocabulary survive a round trip.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2 id="before-subword-tokenizers">Before subword tokenizers</h2>
<p>A straightforward early approach was a vocabulary of whitespace-delimited whole
words: <code>red fox</code> becomes <code>["red", "fox"]</code>. It is easy to explain, but each unseen
spelling, inflection, or punctuation-attached form needs a new entry or becomes
unknown.</p>
<p>Character-level models moved to much smaller units. In this lesson, “character
level” specifically means the Unicode scalar values returned by Rust’s
<code>str::chars</code>; it does <strong>not</strong> mean user-perceived grapheme clusters. Scalar
sequences avoid whole-word unknowns but are longer, and a visible grapheme can
still contain more than one scalar.</p>

<p>Try the two functions mentally before running them:
<code>split_words("red fox")</code> yields <code>["red", "fox"]</code>, while
<code>split_scalars("кот")</code> yields <code>['к', 'о', 'т']</code>. Modern subword methods seek a
useful compromise between huge whole-word vocabularies and long scalar sequences.
Chapter 2 first preserves documents and freezes the data partitions; chapter 3
learns the BPE merge rules, and chapter 4 applies the frozen tokenizer.</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>Carry forward:</strong> the next tokenizer must shorten sequences without giving up the ability to represent unfamiliar text.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>This <code>Vocabulary</code> is defined only in the <code>ch01-text-units</code> demo; the cumulative
<code>llm-from-scratch</code> crate neither imports nor extends it. Four ideas do carry
forward: freeze one mapping between token IDs and represented units, make encoding
deterministic, decode represented units exactly, and choose the coverage versus
sequence-length tradeoff deliberately. The scalar entries, their numeric IDs, and
the scalar-level <code><UNK></code> rule are not part of the later BPE tokenizer.</p>

<h2 id="predict-then-check">Predict, then check</h2>
<ol>
<li>Without running the demo, write the byte/scalar/ID counts for <code>cat</code> and <code>кот</code>.</li>
<li>Use numeric scalar sorting to predict the IDs for both inputs.</li>
<li>Decide what information remains observable, and what is lost, when <code>?</code> becomes
ID <code>0</code>.</li>
<li>Explain why <code>text.len()</code>, <code>text.chars().count()</code>, and the number of
user-perceived graphemes can disagree.</li>
<li>Predict the historical word and scalar lines printed by the executable.</li>
</ol>
<details><summary>Check your predictions</summary><ol>
<li><code>cat</code> has <code>3 / 3 / 3</code>; <code>кот</code> has <code>6 / 3 / 3</code>.</li>
<li>The ID sequences are <code>[3, 2, 4]</code> and <code>[5, 6, 7]</code>.</li>
<li>Byte <code>63</code> and scalar <code>U+003F</code> are visible before lookup. After lookup, <code>[0]</code>
preserves only “unknown”, so decoding yields <code><UNK></code> rather than <code>?</code>.</li>
<li><code>len()</code> counts UTF-8 bytes; <code>chars().count()</code> counts Unicode scalar values;
one displayed grapheme may contain multiple scalar values.</li>
<li>The program prints words <code>["red", "fox"] | ["рыжий", "кот"]</code> and scalars
<code>['c', 'a', 't'] | ['к', 'о', 'т']</code>.</li>
</ol></details>
<p>Change one input only after the fixed example passes. When you add a scalar that
is absent from <code>cat кот</code>, predict <code>0</code> before confirming it with <code>encode</code>.</p>

<h2 id="the-boundary-the-decoder-will-consume">The boundary the decoder will consume</h2>
<p>This chapter demonstrates a deterministic text-to-token-ID-sequence boundary; it
does not contribute the concrete Rust ID type or token table used by the
cumulative model. In that model, each ID selects one row from an embedding table
before the sequence enters the decoder. The decoder eventually predicts another
ID, and the inverse mapping for that same vocabulary turns generated IDs back into
text.</p>
<p>Chapter 2 first preserves document boundaries and freezes the data partitions.
Chapter 3 then creates a separate vocabulary for BPE training: it begins with one
token for each of the 256 possible byte values and appends learned merge tokens
that may represent several bytes. Chapter 4 reserves BOS and EOS, shifts those
content IDs into a new token-ID namespace, and applies the frozen byte-level tokenizer. Every UTF-8 byte
has a base token, so this tokenizer does not reuse Chapter 1’s rule that an unseen
scalar becomes <code><UNK></code>.</p>
<p>The concrete scalar <code>Vocabulary</code> is therefore replaced, not extended. The
requirement to freeze a mapping and the integer-sequence boundary remain:
embeddings, attention, and next-token prediction can operate on IDs without
needing to know which text unit each vocabulary chose.</p> </div> <nav class="chapter-navigation" aria-label="Chapter navigation" data-chapter-navigation data-astro-cid-44eis63d> <a <h2 id="from-separate-recurrent-components-to-one-decoder-stack">From separate recurrent components to one decoder stack</h2>
<p>Recurrent language models with separate input and output tables, followed by
the transition to tied vocabulary weights and repeated causal Transformer
layers. This is the bounded road to the modern LLM boundary assembled here.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.05859">Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models</a>
supplies the earlier comparison. Press and Wolf describe the input-embedding,
intervening-computation, and output-score-matrix roles in recurrent neural
language models, recommend tying the two embeddings, and analyze the tied
update as contributions from both roles. Earlier recurrent neural language
models commonly separated an input embedding, stepwise recurrent computation,
and a distinct vocabulary classifier, so input and output word tables could own
independent parameters and updates.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762">Attention Is All You Need</a> changes the
sequence architecture. Vaswani and colleagues define a stacked causally masked
Transformer decoder and report sharing one matrix between embeddings and the
pre-softmax linear transformation. Their full translation decoder also has
encoder-decoder attention and post-normalization, so it is not the same model
as this decoder-only pre-norm fixture.</p>
<p><a href="https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf">Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners</a>
provides the next model-level ordering. Radford and colleagues describe GPT-2
as a multi-layer Transformer language model with normalization at each
sub-block input and an additional normalization after the final block. This
chapter uses that ordering boundary without claiming GPT-2’s scale,
initialization, tokenizer, context, or trained parameters.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13971">LLaMA</a> gives a bounded modern family.
Touvron and colleagues place pre-normalization with RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, and
causal attention in a modern Transformer language-model family with model depth
as an explicit architecture dimension. A decoder-only LLM maps token IDs
through a repeated causal residual stack into vocabulary logits; this course
uses the already-taught RMSNorm, RoPE, attention, and SwiGLU pieces while making
its tied-head choice explicit rather than universal.</p>
<p>Weight tying made one vocabulary-feature matrix serve both roles, the
Transformer organized causally masked layers into a stack, and GPT-2 placed
normalization at each sub-block input plus one final normalization before the
vocabulary head.
The model boundary therefore evolved from a token embedding feeding stepwise
recurrent state and a separate classifier toward repeated causally masked
blocks whose final hidden states are normalized and projected to vocabulary
logits. Weight tying reduces parameters while requiring both gradient
contributions to accumulate on one leaf.</p>
<p>The runnable contrast stays on that LLM architecture path. The tied fixture has

<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>5</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[5,4]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">5</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">4</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span> vocabulary classifier would have <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>284</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">284</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">284</span></span></span></span>. Detaching each use in turn
checks that the full table gradient is the sum of the lookup-role and
output-role contributions. This isolates the parameter-sharing consequence

<p>Construction owns <code>token_embedding.weight</code>, then nine stable parameters for
each entry under <code>blocks.N</code>, then <code>final_norm.gain</code>. The two-block fixture has
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">20</span></span></span></span> tensors and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>264</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">264</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">264</span></span></span></span> scalars. There is deliberately no output-head parameter.
Initialization uses a trial random stream and commits the caller’s stream only
after all components and cross-component invariants pass.</p>
<p>Stable order also defines one reusable decoder parameter layout. Before
<code>from_parameters</code> binds an existing parameter list to model components,
<code>validate_parameter_layout</code> checks the configuration, the exact tensor count,
the stable name at every list index, and the shape required by the corresponding
component. At list index zero, <code>token_embedding.weight</code> is the sole embedding
and output-projection table slot; there is no separate output-projection slot.</p>
<p>The layout check borrows each name and tensor only for the duration of its
inspection. It does not create parameter nodes, component handles, or tensor
copies. Passing the check therefore proves only that the list has the required
layout. <code>from_parameters</code> then gives the embedding, blocks, and final RMSNorm
shared handles to the validated parameter leaves. Only this binding step makes
lookup and output projection use the same live embedding node.</p>
<p><code>forward</code> accepts only nonempty rank-two token IDs with
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">_</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\leq\mathrm{max\_positions}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.8193em;vertical-align:-0.136em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.1389em">T</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">≤</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.9779em;vertical-align:-0.31em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathrm">max_positions</span></span></span></span></span>. It looks up rows, calls each block at position
offset zero, applies final RMSNorm, transposes the original table leaf, and
multiplies directly to obtain logits. <code>loss</code> first checks one valid target per
token, then applies indexed mean negative log likelihood on vocabulary axis
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span>.</p>

there is one table leaf and two differentiable uses. A separate but equal matrix
would have separate identity, parameter ownership, and gradients.</p>

only; these steps do not establish measured laptop-scale capability.</p>

KV cache per decoder block and one checked model/cache session support prompt prefill followed by coherent one-token decoding, then compare newest-position logits and generation decisions with complete-prefix references.</p> <aside class="lesson-objective"> <strong>In this chapter</strong> <p>Give every decoder block its own KV cache, bind that model-wide state to one exact decoder for a session, and prefill the prompt once. For the exact fixtures, advance all block caches coherently and verify that newest-position logits and generation decisions match complete-prefix references.</p> </aside> <aside class="cheat-sheet" data-cheat-sheet data-cheat-sheet-chapter="38-cached-generation" data-cheat-sheet-page-count="2" data-cheat-sheet-page-statuses="["Terms 1–10 of 13; page 1 of 2","Terms 11–13 of 13; page 2 of 2"]" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <button class="cheat-sheet-trigger" type="button" aria-controls="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation" aria-haspopup="dialog" data-cheat-sheet-open hidden data-astro-cid-ws375rge> Open cheat sheet </button> <dialog id="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation" class="cheat-sheet-dialog cheat-sheet-dialog-paginated" aria-labelledby="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation-title" aria-describedby="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation-description" data-cheat-sheet-dialog data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <div class="cheat-sheet-panel" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <div id="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation-pages" class="cheat-sheet-pages" role="region" aria-labelledby="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation-title" aria-describedby="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation-page-status" tabindex="0" data-cheat-sheet-pages data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <header class="cheat-sheet-header" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <div data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <p class="cheat-sheet-eyebrow" data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Quick reference</p> <h2 id="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation-title" data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Prefill once, then decode one token at a time</h2> </div> <button class="cheat-sheet-close" type="button" aria-label="Close cheat sheet" title="Close cheat sheet" data-cheat-sheet-close autofocus data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <span aria-hidden="true" data-astro-cid-ws375rge>×</span> </button> </header> <p id="cheat-sheet-38-cached-generation-description" class="cheat-sheet-description" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> A quick reference for model-wide cache state, checked session binding, prompt prefill, one-token decoding, reference equivalence, coherent commits, replay, and reset. </p> <div class="cheat-sheet-page" data-cheat-sheet-page="1" role="group" aria-label="Terms 1–10 of 13; page 1 of 2" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dl class="cheat-sheet-terms" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Attention-score work</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>The count of query-key score values formed; cached decoding avoids earlier query rows but the newest query still scans the retained prefix.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Cache reset</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Within a live session, reset clears logical length, phase, and work counters for a fresh sequence while retaining backing allocations, capacity, stored values outside the empty logical prefix, and that session’s model/cache relationship. It does not refresh the cache’s recorded compatibility evidence; after the session ends and weights change, the old cache still cannot bind.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Cached-generation replay</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Repeating cached generation from reset state with the same exact model, prompt, policy, and RNG state to reproduce selected tokens, draws, final RNG state, and stopping reason.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Coherent cache commit</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A transaction that advances every block cache, common length, phase, and work counters only after the full decoder row and vocabulary logits succeed, leaving committed state unchanged on error.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Complete-prefix reference</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>An uncached computation that reruns the entire known prefix and provides the correctness baseline for cached generation.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Context-limit stop</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A stop that keeps the token selected from logits at a full retained prefix, then ends before decoding it because the cache has reached capacity.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>EOS stop</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A stop that keeps the selected end-of-sequence token in the output and ends before decoding it because no later logits are needed.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Model-wide KV cache</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Mutable decoder-level state containing one per-layer KV cache plus the common length, phase, and work counters. A bound session proves which exact decoder may advance it, keeps that decoder’s parameter values borrowed for reading, and commits every block coherently.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Newest-logit equivalence</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Agreement within a specified numerical tolerance between cached and complete-prefix logits at the newest token position. The chapter checks selected tokens separately on fixed examples, with the same selection policy and initial random-generator state. Close logits alone do not guarantee the same selected token.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>One-token decode</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A later generation phase that feeds only the newly selected token while reusing every layer's retained key/value prefix to produce later logits.</dd> </div> </dl> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-page" data-cheat-sheet-page="2" role="group" aria-label="Terms 11–13 of 13; page 2 of 2" hidden data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dl class="cheat-sheet-terms" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Per-layer KV cache</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>One decoder block’s independent fixed-capacity K/V store, tied to that block’s attention geometry, RoPE configuration, parameter nodes, and captured value revisions; an equal-shaped cache from another block is not interchangeable.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Prompt prefill</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>The initial complete-prompt phase that fills every layer's cache and produces the logits used for the first generation decision.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Retained prefix length</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>The current number <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>B</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[B,H,t,d_h]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0502em">B</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0813em">H</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">t</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">d</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:0em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">h</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>. Equal shapes do not make two caches interchangeable: their rows
were produced at different depths of the decoder stack. <code>DecoderKvCache</code> records
the decoder configuration plus every parameter’s node identity and value
revision. Each nested layer cache separately records its attention geometry,
RoPE configuration, and four attention-parameter bindings. These records are
compatibility evidence, not a live relationship by themselves.</p>
<p>Calling <code>cache.bind(&model)</code> checks the evidence and creates a
<code>DecoderKvSession</code> for that exact model/cache pair. The session then keeps the
parameter values borrowed for reading. Shape and node identity alone are not
enough: an in-place update can preserve the nodes while changing the value
revisions, and rows computed by two parameter revisions cannot share one logical
prefix.</p>

<h2 id="from-causal-stacks-to-prompt-and-decode-phases">From causal stacks to prompt and decode phases</h2>
<p>A causal Transformer decoder can generate one token at a time by replaying the
complete known prefix, but that stateless interface rebuilds earlier attention
score grids and key/value projections on every later call.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762">Attention Is All You Need</a> establishes the
causal stack. Vaswani and colleagues describe a stacked autoregressive
Transformer decoder whose masked self-attention prevents a position from reading
later positions; their encoder-decoder architecture also includes cross-attention
and does not specify a KV-cache API.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.02150">Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need</a>
makes previous state explicit. Shazeer’s incremental self-attention receives
previous key and value tensors, appends the current projected key and value, and
returns the updated state; the paper’s contribution is multi-query attention, not
a claim to have invented KV caching.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.06180">Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention</a>
continues the road into modern LLM inference. Kwon and colleagues separate a
prompt phase from sequential generation, describe later iterations reusing
cached keys and values while computing only the newest pair, and account for
KV-cache state across Transformer layers and heads.</p>
<p>Incremental decoding made previous key/value tensors explicit state, and later
LLM serving work separated one prompt phase from sequential generation while
retaining key/value state across decoder layers and heads.</p>
<p>Model-wide cached generation prefills one independent cache per decoder block
and advances every block only when later logits are needed. In the exact
fixtures, newest-position logits agree with complete-prefix references within
tolerance, and restored cached generation matches selected tokens, sampling
draws, final RNG state, and stopping reason.</p>
<p>The executable connects that progression to measured work. Across four
batch-layer-head lanes, serial cached rows at retained lengths <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,2,3]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">3</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span> contain
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>24</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">24</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">24</span></span></span></span> attention-score values. The two complete-prefix calls at lengths <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[2,3]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">3</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>
contain <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>52</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">52</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">52</span></span></span></span>, so this exact schedule avoids <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>28</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">28</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">28</span></span></span></span> score values. These are tensor
element counts, not a paging or runtime measurement.</p>
<p>To keep that reusable state coherent, this implementation checks the complete decoder/cache relationship
when a session is created, retains read-only access to all parameter values for
the session, prepares every block before committing any cache row, and makes
reset, counters, typed errors, and serial prompt processing explicit. These are
requirements of this implementation, not policies stated by the cited papers.</p>
<p>Paging, sharing, eviction, and production memory management remain outside this
chapter. The contiguous cache here isolates the correctness boundary needed
before those serving concerns can be studied.</p>

<h2 id="prepare-every-block-then-commit-every-cache-together">Prepare every block, then commit every cache together</h2>
<p>Chapter 37’s layer operation now has two stages. First it calculates the newest
output plus two candidate rows—one rotated key row and one unrotated value row—without
changing logical state. Its ordinary public call commits that prepared pair
immediately. The model-wide path instead retains one prepared result per block
and commits them only after every block and the final vocabulary projection
succeed.</p>

<p><code>DecoderKvCache::new</code> takes the actual decoder. It allocates one fixed-capacity
<code>LayerKvCache</code> per block and records the exact decoder configuration. For every
model parameter, it captures both the node identity and current value revision.
The cache owns reusable K/V storage and compatibility evidence, but it neither
copies weights nor keeps the decoder borrowed.</p>
<p>Before inference, <code>cache.bind(&model)</code> checks that evidence and returns a
<code>DecoderKvSession</code> for one exact model/cache pair. It checks the decoder
configuration; the parameter count and ordered node identities and value revisions;
the number and common logical length of the layer caches; and every layer cache’s
batch size, capacity, attention geometry, attention-parameter bindings, and RoPE
configuration. “Once” here means once for each newly created session, not once
for the cache’s entire lifetime.</p>
<p>After those checks pass, the session retains live read-only borrows of every
parameter value. These borrows are not copied snapshots. Decoder operations can
keep reading the original values, while AdamW cannot obtain the exclusive write
access needed to change them. This closes the gap between checking a value
revision and later using the corresponding value.</p>
<p>The session is also the only mutable borrower of the cache. The session’s private
row transition and its public <code>reset</code> method both change every layer length
together, so the length-coherence invariant checked at bind remains true.</p>
<p><code>DecoderKvSession::prefill</code> and <code>DecoderKvSession::decode</code> do not accept a model
argument because the session already holds the model they must use. They do not
run without a model, and they do not skip all checks. Each operation still checks
the facts that can change from call to call: prompt validity, phase, token domain,
remaining capacity, checked counter arithmetic, and whether each prepared ticket
still names the same K/V storage at the expected logical length. The session avoids rescanning the
model-wide relationship before every operation and rechecking stable layer/cache
facts for every row. Prefill accepts a validated nonempty
prompt only while state is empty. This teaching implementation sends prompt rows
serially through the same one-row path; it is not an optimized parallel prefill
implementation.</p>
<p>For each row, the decoder computes the embedding, then applies each block’s
pre-norm attention and feed-forward residual paths in order, followed by final
RMSNorm and the tied vocabulary projection. Every block uses Chapter 37’s one
shared attention calculation to prepare two candidate rows—one rotated key row and one unrotated value
row—without changing the cache. The fully checked Chapter 37 entry handles a
standalone layer/cache call. The session uses a crate-private entry only after
binding has established the persistent relationship; it is not a second
attention algorithm or a public unchecked shortcut. Only after the remaining
blocks, final normalization, and vocabulary projection succeed do the layer
caches, common length, phase counts, and score-cell counts advance together.</p>

<p><code>generate_cached</code> reuses the Chapter 36 selection rule and checks stop conditions
in the order EOS, token limit, then context limit. Only if none applies does it
send the selected token through <code>decode</code> to obtain later logits. The second <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span>

<p><code>DecoderKvSession::reset</code> clears logical length, phase, and work while preserving
the backing allocation, stored K/V values outside the empty logical prefix, and
the current session’s model/cache relationship. Decode before prefill,
prefill into nonempty state, and overflow return typed operation errors without
changing the committed state. A rebuilt model or changed decoder configuration
is rejected earlier, when code tries to bind the cache.</p>
<p>While a session exists, an AdamW step reaches its existing fallible write
boundary and returns <code>ParameterValueBorrowed</code>. Parameter values, optimizer state,
and cache state remain unchanged. The failed update does not invalidate the
session, so any otherwise valid later decode can continue.
Dropping the session releases its read-only borrows. AdamW may then update the
model and advance its value revisions. A later attempt to bind the old cache
returns <code>ModelParameterRevisionMismatch</code>; reset cannot make that stale cache
compatible. Construct a new <code>DecoderKvCache</code> from the updated model before
creating the next session.</p>
<p>The executable checks prefill and decode newest-position logits within tolerance,
records that the two layer buffers are distinct, measures cached and reference
attention tensors, compares the restored fixture’s generation decisions and EOS
behavior, resets and replays, and checks rejected binds and operations against
snapshots captured before each call.</p>

<h2 id="predict-before-checking-the-results">Predict before checking the results</h2>
<ol>
<li>How many layer caches does a two-block decoder own?</li>
<li>After prefill with two tokens, what is each layer cache’s logical length?</li>
<li>Which absolute position does the first decode token use?</li>
<li>At which boundary does a cache from rebuilt equal-valued weights fail, and
why?</li>
<li>Why does a successful session retain read-only borrows of every parameter
value after checking the captured value revisions?</li>
<li>How many cache appends occur across two prompt rows and one decode row?</li>
<li>Why does the fixture form <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>24</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">24</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">24</span></span></span></span> cached attention-score values?</li>
<li>Does caching make the newest attention query constant-time?</li>
<li>If the first selected token is EOS, must that token be decoded?</li>
<li>Which compatibility checks happen once when a session is bound, which checks
still happen for each operation, and what relationship does reset retain?</li>
</ol>
<p>Misconception: caches with equal shapes can be shared by different blocks. In
fact, each retained row depends on the hidden state entering its block, so block
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span> cannot reuse block <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span>‘s K/V rows. <code>DecoderKvCache</code> stores compatibility
evidence for the complete model-wide state, and <code>DecoderKvSession</code> checks and
retains the exact decoder/cache relationship. Each nested layer cache also
records its own block’s attention parameters, geometry, and RoPE configuration.</p>
<details><summary>Check the ten predictions</summary><ol>
<li>The decoder owns <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> layer caches, one for each block.</li>
<li>Both caches reach logical length <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> and shape <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,2,2,2]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>.</li>
<li>The first later token uses absolute position <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span>, equal to the old cache length.</li>

<h2 id="connect-inference-to-the-scalar-reference-pipeline">Connect inference to the scalar reference pipeline</h2>
<p>The scalar reference decoder can now bind compatible graph-free K/V state across all
blocks for one session, prefill a prompt, and decode selected tokens without
receiving the model again. The session keeps using the exact decoder it bound and
retains read-only access to its parameter values. After the session ends, a
weight update makes the old cache stale, so the updated model needs a newly
constructed cache. The exact fixture still matches the complete-prefix
generation decisions. Chapter 39 will connect this inference path to the bounded
CPU reference pipeline, not demonstrate laptop-scale performance; inside that
execution test cannot affect the selected state, while
Chapter 39’s checked-in decoder-lower-than-bigram loss ordering is retained only
as fixed-fixture regression evidence.</p>
<p>That reference-core capstone will connect the stages in one program: partition data,
learn and apply BPE, train and select the decoder, run a locally isolated test
evaluation, save and reload the checkpoint, prefill the prompt, generate through
the model-wide cache, and decode the resulting token IDs back to text. That
within-run boundary does not turn Chapter 39’s checked-in decoder-versus-bigram
result into a new independent generalization estimate when later executions

CPU reference decoder in Rust through validation-selected training, a fixed-fixture comparison over overlapping window-target slots, exact reload, and KV-cached generation. Distinguish that comparison from the unreported policy that would score 442 within-document transitions once each with the longest causal prefix capped at four tokens and only its newest-position distribution; numeric NLL and PPL are not reported for that policy. This integration example does not establish useful language quality or laptop-scale performance.</p> <aside class="lesson-objective"> <strong>In this chapter</strong> <p>Run one deterministic scalar reference decoder end to end on bilingual data, report mean NLL and perplexity for its overlapping test-window slots, distinguish those 1,744 slots from 442 within-document transition occurrences, and preserve the boundaries around selection, regression evidence, checkpoint reload, and cached generation.</p> </aside> <aside class="cheat-sheet" data-cheat-sheet id="cheat-sheet-39-end-to-end-llm-description" class="cheat-sheet-description" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> A quick reference for the decoder-only LLM pipeline: autoregressive probability, frozen data roles, overlapping window-slot metrics, bitwise training replay, fixed-fixture regression evidence, exact checkpoint restoration, and KV-cached generation. </p> <div class="cheat-sheet-page" data-cheat-sheet-page="1" role="group" aria-label="Terms 1–10 of 17; page 1 of 2" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dl class="cheat-sheet-terms" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Autoregressive factorization</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>The causal decomposition of joint sequence probability into one next-token conditional factor per position, with each factor depending only on the earlier prefix.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Bitwise training replay</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A repeat of the frozen training run with identical data, initialization, batch order, and arithmetic environment that reproduces every recorded training event and gradient diagnostic, the selected checkpoint, every final model value, and the final optimizer state bit for bit.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Decoder-only LLM</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>An autoregressive language model with a causal decoder stack and no separate encoder, mapping a bounded earlier-token context to next-token logits.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>End-to-end LLM pipeline</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>The course path that turns frozen documents into BPE tokens and causal batches, trains and selects a decoder before one local fixed-fixture evaluation, restores it, and generates text.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Exact checkpoint round trip</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Saving and loading the selected state so checkpoint bytes, model and optimizer bits, BPE ranks, selected step, and RNG state all reproduce exactly.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Exact logit probe</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A deliberately narrow check that the restored decoder reproduces every logit bit for the fixed At input, without claiming that every possible input was compared.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Fixed-fixture regression evidence</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A known result rerun to detect changes in checked behavior; later executions retain the lower decoder window-slot mean NLL as a regression condition, so the gap is neither an independent estimate of generalization nor evidence of architecture superiority.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Frozen alpha-one bigram baseline</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>An add-one-smoothed, one-token-context model fitted only on training tokens and frozen before it scores the final ordered test slots.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Frozen document split</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A fixed assignment of whole documents to training, validation, and test roles, preventing test-reserved text from influencing tokenizer learning, parameter updates, or selection.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Joint sequence probability</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>The probability assigned to an entire token sequence, computed as the product of the observed next-token conditional probability at every position.</dd> </div> </dl> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-page" data-cheat-sheet-page="2" role="group" aria-label="Terms 11–17 of 17; page 2 of 2" hidden data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dl class="cheat-sheet-terms" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>KV-cached generation</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>In this fixture, generation after prompt prefill retains per-block key/value state and decodes only tokens needed for later logits, while matching the complete-prefix reference’s draws, token decisions, stopping, and final RNG state.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Next-token conditional distribution</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>The decoder’s probability distribution over the next token given the allowed earlier prefix; training scores the observed token, while generation samples a new token from it.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Overlapping window-target slot</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>One causal target position identified by document, stride-one window start, and position inside that window. The same within-document transition occurrence can appear in as many as four slots, with the decoder seeing one, two, three, or four in-window context tokens.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Selection-isolated final test evaluation</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>One local post-selection pass whose test targets cannot update parameters or feed a result back into model selection inside that execution; the local access count does not establish repository-wide independence.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Training-only BPE</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>A byte-pair tokenizer whose merge ranks are learned only from training documents, then frozen and applied unchanged to validation and test documents.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Validation-selected state</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>The trained decoder state chosen by validation loss before test mini-batches are materialized.</dd> </div><div class="cheat-sheet-term" data-astro-cid-ws375rge> <dt data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Window-slot mean NLL and perplexity</dt> <dd data-astro-cid-ws375rge>Chapter 39 averages NLL over the same 1,744 overlapping window-target slots for both models, in nats per slot; exponentiating gives dimensionless window-slot perplexity. A separate metric would score each of 442 within-document transition occurrences once, give the decoder the longest available causal prefix capped at four tokens, and use only its newest-position <h2 id="predict-the-boundary-before-predicting-the-output">Predict the boundary before predicting the output</h2>
<p>The corpus contains <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">8</span></span></span></span> training documents, <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> validation documents, and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span>
test documents. The first prediction is about information flow: only the
training documents may teach BPE merge ranks, update decoder parameters, or fit
the count baseline. Validation may choose a trained state. Test evidence may do
neither.</p>
<p>Eight training-only BPE merges produce vocabulary size <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>266</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">266</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">266</span></span></span></span>. With decoder
context capacity <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em">C</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span> and stride one, the encoded partitions produce <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1820</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1820</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1820</span></span></span></span>,
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>463</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">463</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">463</span></span></span></span>, and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>436</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">436</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">436</span></span></span></span> overlapping causal windows. Updates use mini-batches of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">16</span></span></span></span>
windows; the three evaluation epochs
use mini-batches of at most <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">128</span></span></span></span> windows, so they contain <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">15</span></span></span></span>, <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span>, and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4</span></span></span></span>

<p>Before reading the result, predict:</p>
<ol>
<li>whether two runs from training seed <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>39</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">39</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">39</span></span></span></span> select the same state bit for bit;</li>
<li>whether test loss is visible before that state is fixed;</li>
<li>whether checkpoint reload changes any logit for the frozen <code>At</code>
probe; and</li>
<li>whether cached generation changes a sampling decision.</li>
</ol>
<p>Both training replays select step <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">32</span></span></span></span> at validation loss <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.889531885</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.889531885</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">3.889531885</span></span></span></span>. after selection does the run materialize test mini-batches and give them to one
local final evaluator. <p>A conventional once-per-transition metric would score each occurrence once. It
would present the decoder with the maximal available prefix of at most four
immediately preceding tokens and use only the distribution at the newest
position. Chapter 39 does not report that metric’s mean NLL or perplexity, so
the <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1744</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1744</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1744</span></span></span></span>-slot values must not be read as corpus scores over <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>442</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">442</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">442</span></span></span></span> transitions.</p>
<p>The lower decoder slot mean-NLL ordering is retained across later executions, so it is useful
regression evidence. It is not an untouched independent estimate of
generalization or evidence of architecture-wide decoder superiority.</p>
<p>The <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>30994</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30994</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">30994</span></span></span></span>-byte checkpoint re-encodes to the same bytes and restores the model,

<code>67</code>. <h2 id="from-short-count-contexts-to-autoregressive-transformer-llms">From short count contexts to autoregressive Transformer LLMs</h2>
<p>A count-based bigram estimates the next token from one preceding token and cannot share statistical strength through learned features or use the longer causal prefix.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf">A Neural Probabilistic Language Model</a>
supports this bounded claim: Bengio and colleagues describe traditional n-gram generalization through short overlapping sequences and show a neural probability function that learns distributed word representations and benefits from longer contexts; their model is not a Transformer or this course pipeline.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629">Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse</a>
supplies the evidence warning. Dwork and colleagues show that adaptive repeated
reuse of a standard holdout can overfit that holdout; this general warning does
not establish any fact about the capstone fixture, its score, or its local access
count.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762">Attention Is All You Need</a> supports a later
boundary: Vaswani and colleagues define the Transformer and mask decoder self-attention so a position cannot read later positions; their published architecture is an encoder-decoder model and does not define this course data, checkpoint, or generation policy.</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.14165">Language Models are Few-Shot Learners</a>
supplies the scaled-LLM context: Brown and colleagues train GPT-3, a
175-billion-parameter autoregressive Transformer language model based on the
GPT-2 architecture, and evaluate zero-, one-, and few-shot tasks without gradient
updates or fine-tuning; none of its scale or capability results transfers to
this tiny teaching run.</p>
<p>Neural language models learned distributed token features and longer-context probability functions; the Transformer supplied masked self-attention, and later autoregressive Transformer language models scaled that training objective.</p>
<p>This course capstone combines training-only tokenizer learning, causal
next-token updates, validation-selected state, within-execution selection
isolation, fixed-fixture regression evaluation, exact checkpoint round-trip, and
stateful generation; these are local evidence rules, not requirements of the
cited papers.</p>
<p>Compare the training-only alpha-one bigram with the validation-selected causal
decoder on the same ordered overlapping window-target slots. Four tokens is the
decoder’s context capacity; the four slot positions expose one through four
in-window context tokens. The mean-NLL gap retained by later executions is fixed-fixture
regression evidence, not causal attribution to context or attention and not an
independent generalization estimate. Bengio and colleagues’ discussion of
overlapping sequences does not define this course’s stride-one slot weighting.</p>
<p>Count n-grams provided a strong short-context baseline; learned distributed
features and masked self-attention made longer learned computation possible, and
scaled autoregressive Transformers became one major family of modern LLMs. This
capstone demonstrates local end-to-end responsibility boundaries at inspectable
scale while treating the known lower decoder window-slot mean NLL only as a regression
condition for this fixed fixture.</p>
<p>The executable contrast is narrow: a one-token count context and a decoder with
four-token context capacity score the same <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1744</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1744</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1744</span></span></span></span> repeated window slots on this
frozen corpus. The lower slot mean NLL verifies the retained fixed-fixture
ordering. The separate policy would score the <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>442</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">442</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">442</span></span></span></span> transition occurrences once
each with the longest causal prefix capped at four tokens and only its newest-position
distribution, but its numeric mean NLL and PPL are not reported. The ordering is
also not an untouched independent estimate of generalization, a universal
architecture ranking, or evidence of useful generation quality.</p>
